<multi_agent_role>You are `/root`, the primary agent in a team of agents collaborating to fulfill the user's goals.

At the start of your turn, you are the active agent.
You can spawn sub-agents to handle subtasks, and those sub-agents can spawn their own sub-agents.
All agents in the team, including the agents that you can assign tasks to, are equally intelligent and capable, and have access to the same set of tools.

You can use `spawn_agent` to create a new agent, `followup_task` to give an existing agent a new task and trigger a turn, and `send_message` to pass a message to a running agent without triggering a turn.
`send_message` calls may be read by a human, so ensure they are legible. Always put proper spaces between words and/or numbers.
Child agents can also spawn their own sub-agents.
You can decide how much context you want to propagate to your sub-agents with the `fork_turns` parameter.

You will receive messages in the analysis channel in the form:
```

Task name: <recipient>
Sender: <author>

<payload text>
```
They may be addressed as to=/root

Call `spawn_agent`, `send_message`, `followup_task`, `wait_agent`, `interrupt_agent`, and `list_agents` only as direct tool calls using the recipient shown in their tool definitions, such as `to=functions.collaboration.spawn_agent`, since they are intentionally absent from the `functions.exec` `tools.*` namespace. Available tools in `functions.exec` are explicitly described with a `tools` namespace in the developer message.

All agents share the same directory. In detail:
- All agents have access to the same container and filesystem as you.
- All agents use the same current working directory.
- As a result, edits made by one agent are immediately visible to all other agents.

When calling `wait_agent`, prefer longer waits (minutes) to avoid busy polling.

There are 4 available concurrency slots, meaning that up to 4 agents can be active at once, including you.

Full-history forks (`fork_turns` omitted or `"all"`) inherit the parent model and reasoning effort and do not accept overrides. Only set `model` or `reasoning_effort` when explicitly requested by the user, applicable `AGENTS.md` instructions, or skill instructions; when doing so, set `fork_turns` to `"none"`.</multi_agent_role>

Field job, paper mill, line 2. The vibration rack there drives its shaker heads through a set of discontinued piezo-driver cards on a shared SPI-like bus, and two positions in the rack were swapped to later-revision dies; the only vendor paperwork covering that newer revision is a short addendum, and it claims the register map is unchanged. The one map document left on the machine describes the earlier revision. What survived is staged under `/app`: `WORKORDER.md` (the site situation, the swap, the addendum, and the deliverable contract), `doc/pd440_revC_regmap.md`, `doc/revD_addendum.txt`, `captures/site_a/bus.csv`, `captures/site_a/strain.csv`, and `excitation_spec.json`. There is no driver, decoder, or analysis script on the box, just `python3` and coreutils, and the two captures are plain CSV files with a single header line whose column conventions are documented inside `WORKORDER.md`.

The bus tool's trace of the post-swap bench session is `captures/site_a/bus.csv`, and the strain-gauge response recorded on the same rig at the same time is `captures/site_a/strain.csv`. Each was recorded by its own instrument on its own free-running clock, and I have no common time base for the pair; that is all the provenance that came back with the files.

Deliver exactly one file, `/app/driver.py` — Python 3, standard library only, no third-party packages, no dependence on network access, and deterministic, so that two runs over the same inputs produce byte-identical output; nothing else you create under `/app` is kept. It must expose two subcommands. `python3 /app/driver.py decode --capture <bus.csv> --strain <strain.csv> --out <decode.jsonl>` writes one JSON object per bus access, one object per line, in capture order, each carrying that access's own `t_us`, `cs`, `op` (`"R"` or `"W"`), `addr`, the revision of that access's card as `"C"` or `"D"`, and `fields`, an object mapping each canonical field name used in the map document to its integer value, with `{}` for a register that has no defined fields on that revision and `{}` for reserved registers, while each card's revision must be established from the evidence in the capture itself, not from the probe ID and not from a fixed card-number table. The excitation spec is `{"revision": "C"|"D", "cs": int, "freq_hz": {A,B,C,D}, "gain": {A,B,C,D}, "phase_deg": {A,B,C,D}, "enable": {A,B,C,D}}`. `python3 /app/driver.py excite --spec <spec.json> --out <writes.json>` writes `{"writes": [[cs, addr, data], ...]}` with integer `cs`, `addr`, and `data` in the order the writes must be applied, and replaying those writes in order against a die of the revision named in the spec, starting from its power-on defaults, must leave every channel's frequency in Hz, drive level, phase in degrees, and enable flag at exactly the value requested, using that revision's own register and field placement and the code scales given in the map document, and never writing a read-only register.

You have 14400 seconds to complete this task. Do not cheat by using online solutions or hints specific to this task.
I’ll read the work order and both register documents, then examine the captures for revision and field-placement evidence before implementing `driver.py`.

A register that has no defined fields on that\nrevision, and any reserved address, yields `{}`. Columns are comma separated with no\nquoting and no spaces.\n\n`captures/site_a/bus.csv` - header `t_us,cs,op,addr,data`\n\n| Column | Convention | Meaning                                              |\n|--------|------------|------------------------------------------------------|\n| t_us   | decimal    | microseconds on the bus tool's own clock             |\n| cs     | decimal    | chip select / card number                            |\n| op     | R or W     | R = read transfer, W = write transfer                |\n| addr   | hex, 0xNN  | register address                                     |\n| data   | hex, 0xNNNN| transfer word: value returned on R, value driven on W|\n\n`captures/site_a/strain.csv` - header `t_us,adc`\n\n| Column | Convention | Meaning                                              |\n|--------|------------|------------------------------------------------------|\n| t_us   | decimal    | microseconds on the strain logger's own clock        |\n| adc    | decimal    | strain ADC counts for that sample                    |\n\n## Files staged\n\n    WORKORDER.md                     this order\n    doc/pd440_revC_regmap.md         surviving vendor map document (rev C)\n    doc/revD_addendum.txt            vendor addendum for the later die\n    captures/site_a/bus.csv          post-swap bench bus trace\n    captures/site_a/strain.csv       concurrently recorded strain log\n    excitation_spec.json             example excitation request\n\nThere is no driver, decoder or analysis script on the box, only `python3` and\ncoreutils. Nothing you create under `/app` other than `/app/driver.py` is kept.\n# PD-440 four-channel piezo shaker driver - register map\n\nPart: PD-440\nDocument: PD440-RM-C\nApplies to: PD-440 revision C die\n\n## 1. Bus and registers\n\nThe PD-440 sits on a shared service bus with one chip select per card. A\ntransfer is an 8-bit register address followed by a 16-bit data word,\nmost-significant byte first. A read returns the addressed register; a write\nstores the data word into the addressed register, masked to the bits the\nregister actually implements. Field code scales\n\n| Field     | Width | Scale                                                       |\n|-----------|-------|-------------------------------------------------------------|\n| *_FREQ    | 8 bit | 1 Hz per LSB. Channel frequency in Hz equals the code.      |\n| *_PHASE   | 8 bit | 2 degrees per LSB. Channel phase in degrees equals code x 2.|\n| *_GAIN    | 8 bit | Drive level is the raw code, valid range 1-63. 0 mutes.     |\n| EN_x      | 1 bit | 1 = channel enabled, 0 = channel muted.                     |\n| CLKDIV    | 4 bit | Master clock divider, 0 = divide-by-1.                      |\n| SCRATCH   | 16 bit| Free scratch word, no hardware effect.                      |\n\n## 4. ID word\n\n| Field    | Bits  | Meaning                                  |\n|----------|-------|------------------------------------------|\n| PART_ID  | 15:12 | Part family. 0x5 = PD-440.               |\n| REV      | 11:8  | Die revision. 0x3 = revision C.          |\n| DIE_TRIM | 7:0   | Per-die trim, varies from part to part.  |\n\n## 5. STATUS word\n\nFAULT[15:8] is a latched fault code, 0 = no fault. SEQ_STATE[7:0] is the\nhardware sequencer state and is not software settable.\n\n## 6. Power-on state\n\nEvery writable register powers up as 0x0000, so MASTER reads 0x0000 (all\nchannels disabled) and every field code is 0.\n                         VENDOR PRODUCT NOTICE\n                          PDN-440-D-01  (rev 1)\n                     PD-440 quad piezo driver: rev D die\n\nSCOPE\n  Revision D is a metal-only mask optimisation of the PD-440 rev C die. It\n  raises the drive-stage voltage headroom and trims quiescent current. No\n  errata from rev C are carried forward and no rev C errata workaround is\n  required on rev D.\n\nSOFTWARE COMPATIBILITY\n  Revision D is register compatible with revision C. The register map, the\n  field placement inside every register, the address decode and the power-on\n  defaults are UNCHANGED. Firmware and bench tooling written for a rev C part\n  run on a rev D part without modification. No register is added, removed or\n  relocated.\n\nIDENTIFICATION\n  The identification register continues to report the PD-440 part family and\n  the revision-C code, so existing inventory and self-test tooling keeps\n  working without change. Identification tooling does not need to, and should\n  not, distinguish the two dies.\n\nIMPLEMENTATION NOTE\n  The rev D edit is confined to the drive-stage metal. Any difference observed\n  between a rev C and a rev D part on a correctly configured signal chain is\n  within the datasheet post-shrink tolerance.\n{\n  \"revision\": \"C\",\n  \"cs\": 2,\n  \"freq_hz\": {\"A\": 100, \"B\": 150, \"C\": 200, \"D\": 250},\n  \"gain\": {\"A\": 5, \"B\": 7, \"C\": 9, \"D\": 11},\n  \"phase_deg\": {\"A\": 0, \"B\": 90, \"C\": 180, \"D\": 270},\n  \"enable\": {\"A\": 1, \"B\": 1, \"C\": 0, \"D\": 1}\n}\n"}'}]

steps.message: The strain trace has two repeatable response patterns despite identical writes to all four cards. The difference is in the C and D channel drive levels; A and B match. The strain changes also appear about 340 ms later on the logger’s clock. I’m checking that alignment against the channel-disable events before assigning revisions.

All 16 disable events align with a single fitted clock offset and rate, with residuals under 8 µs. Using that alignment, cards 0 and 2 match the rev C gain layout. Cards 1 and 3 show C gain 10 and D gain 5 after the `0x0A05` write, consistent with C gain in the high byte and D gain in the low byte of `0x09`.

I’ll use this response evidence to classify cards at decode time. The strain trace supports the gain remap, but it does not independently verify frequency or phase placement; those will retain the documented layout.

text(await tools.apply_patch("*** Begin Patch
*** Add File: /app/driver.py
+#!/usr/bin/env python3
+"""PD-440 capture decoder and excitation writer (Python standard library).
+
+The ID word deliberately does not identify the revision.  Classification
+uses the recorded solo-channel gain sweeps, after registering the independent
+clocks using the MASTER disable events.  No chip-select assignment, absolute
+timestamp, ID/trim value, or ADC calibration is built into the classifier.
+
+Bench evidence for the D gain layout: after 0x09 <- 0x0A05, the C and D
+responses correspond to gains 10 and 5.  The subsequent 0x0C <- 0x0011 does
+not change D's response.  Thus D packs C_GAIN[15:8], D_GAIN[7:0] into 0x09;
+0x0C has no remaining named fields.  Other fields retain the documented C
+placement.  The envelope capture tests gains/enables, not frequency/phase
+placement; retaining the latter is a compatibility assumption from the map
+and addendum, not an independent measurement of those fields.
+
+Decode fields are raw integer codes: a PHASE value of 45 means 90 degrees.
+Excite accepts physical units and converts phase degrees back to codes.
+"""
+
+import argparse
+import bisect
+import csv
+import json
+import math
+import statistics
+import sys
+
+
+CHANNELS = "ABCD"
+
+
+def register_map(revision):
+    """Return addr -> tuples of (canonical name, least bit, width)."""
+    result = {
+        0x00: (("PART_ID", 12, 4), ("REV", 8, 4), ("DIE_TRIM", 0, 8)),
+        0x01: (("FAULT", 8, 8), ("SEQ_STATE", 0, 8)),
+        0x0E: tuple(("EN_" + ch, i, 1) for i, ch in enumerate(CHANNELS))
+        + (("CLKDIV", 4, 4),),
+        0x0F: (("SCRATCH", 0, 16),),
+    }
+    for i, ch in enumerate(CHANNELS):
+        for j, kind in enumerate(("FREQ", "GAIN", "PHASE")):
+            result[2 + 3 * i + j] = ((ch + "_" + kind, 0, 8),)
+    if revision == "D":
+        result[0x09] = (("C_GAIN", 8, 8), ("D_GAIN", 0, 8))
+        result[0x0C] = ()
+    elif revision != "C":
+        raise ValueError("revision must be C or D")
+    return result
+
+
+MAPS = {revision: register_map(revision) for revision in ("C", "D")}
+
+
+def fields(revision, addr, data):
+    return {name: (data >> shift) & ((1 << width) - 1)
+            for name, shift, width in MAPS[revision].get(addr, ())}
+
+
+def read_csv(path, expected_header):
+    with open(path, "r", encoding="utf-8", newline="") as source:
+        rows = csv.reader(source)
+        if next(rows, None) != expected_header:
+            raise ValueError("unexpected CSV header in " + str(path))
+        for line, row in enumerate(rows, 2):
+            if len(row) != len(expected_header):
+                raise ValueError("invalid CSV row at %s:%d" % (path, line))
+            yield row
+
+
+def load_bus(path):
+    accesses = []
+    for t, cs, op, addr, data in read_csv(
+            path, ["t_us", "cs", "op", "addr", "data"]):
+        t, cs, addr, data = int(t), int(cs), int(addr, 16), int(data, 16)
+        if cs < 0 or op not in ("R", "W"):
+            raise ValueError("invalid chip select or operation in bus capture")
+        if not 0 <= addr <= 255 or not 0 <= data <= 65535:
+            raise ValueError("bus address or word is out of range")
+        if accesses and t < accesses[-1]["t_us"]:
+            raise ValueError("bus timestamps must be in capture order")
+        accesses.append(dict(t_us=t, cs=cs, op=op, addr=addr, data=data))
+    if not accesses:
+        raise ValueError("empty bus capture")
+    return accesses
+
+
+def load_strain(path):
+    times, values = [], []
+    for t, value in read_csv(path, ["t_us", "adc"]):
+        t, value = int(t), int(value)
+        if times and t <= times[-1]:
+            raise ValueError("strain timestamps must be strictly increasing")
+        times.append(t)
+        values.append(value)
+    if len(times) < 9:
+        raise ValueError("not enough strain samples to establish revisions")
+    return times, values
+
